items.stem: What is a primary key?
options: A field that links to another table
A field (or fields) that uniquely identifies each record in a table
The first field in every table
items.answer: A field (or fields) that uniquely identifies each record in a table
items.markingKey: Primary key values must be unique and not empty.

items.stem: Explain two limitations of a file-based approach to storing data.
items.answer: Data redundancy — the same data held in several files; data inconsistency — copies updated in one file but not another; data dependency — programs tied to file structure; hard to share/secure data.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per limitation with explanation, max 2 × 2 [4]

items.stem: Explain how a relational database reduces data inconsistency.
items.answer: Data about each entity is stored once in its own table and linked by keys, so an update is made in one place and every query sees the same value.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: stored once; 1 mark: updated in one place/linked by keys [2]

items.stem: Coral Bay Aquarium in Jakarta keeps customer details in one file for the sales team and a separate file of orders for the warehouse. (a) Identify a suitable primary key and foreign key for the ORDER table. (b) Explain how referential integrity prevents errors.
items.answer: (a) Primary key OrderID; foreign key CustomerID. (b) Each foreign key must match an existing primary key so an order cannot refer to a customer who does not exist.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain why a primary key is needed in each table.
items.answer: It uniquely identifies each record so records can be found, updated and linked through foreign keys without ambiguity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: unique identification; 1 mark: linking/searching [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between a primary key and a foreign key.
items.answer: A primary key uniquely identifies records in its own table; a foreign key is an attribute in another table that refers to that primary key to create a relationship.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Lakeside College in Kuala Lumpur keeps customer details in one file for the sales team and a separate file of orders for the warehouse. (a) Explain two problems caused by the file-based approach. (b) Describe how a relational database would be structured instead.
items.answer: (a) Redundancy (same customer details in several files); inconsistency (address updated in one only); difficult to query across files; poor security. (b) Separate tables for each entity (CUSTOMER, ORDER) linked by primary/foreign keys; data stored once.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each problem, 1 mark explanation [4] (b) 1 mark tables; 1 mark keys/link [2]

items.stem: A table is in first normal form (1NF) when
options: every non-key attribute depends on the whole key
it has no repeating groups of attributes and every field is atomic
items.answer: it has no repeating groups of attributes and every field is atomic
items.markingKey: 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups, a primary key.

items.stem: Explain why a many-to-many relationship cannot be implemented directly in a relational database.
items.answer: A foreign key field can hold only one value per record, so each side would need repeating groups; a link table is used to turn it into two one-to-many relationships.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: one value per field/repeating groups; 1 mark: link table [2]

items.stem: Explain the benefits of normalising a database.
items.answer: Reduces data redundancy, so less storage and fewer update anomalies; improves data integrity and consistency.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point, max 2 [2]

items.stem: What is the relationship between the entities DEPARTMENT and EMPLOYEE?
items.answer: one-to-many
items.markingKey: A department has many employees, but each employee works in one department.

items.stem: State the type of relationship between COUNTRY and CAPITAL, giving a reason. Explain how this relationship would be implemented using tables and keys.
items.answer: one-to-one: each country has one capital city and each capital belongs to one country. Implementation: the primary key of one table is a foreign key in the other.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: one-to-one; 1 mark: reason; 1 mark: implementation [3]

items.stem: Freya is designing a database for a car hire company in Cairo. All the data is currently held in one table: HIRE(HireID, CustomerID, CustomerName, CarReg, Make, Model, StartDate, Days). (a) Identify the primary key. (b) Explain why the table is not in 2NF or 3NF, giving an example. (c) Produce a design in 3NF. (d) Explain one benefit of the new design.
items.answer: (a) HireID (b) partial: none, because the primary key is a single field (so the table is already in 2NF once in 1NF); transitive: CustomerName depends on CustomerID and Make/Model depend on CarReg, not directly on HireID (c) CUSTOMER(CustomerID, CustomerName); CAR(CarReg, Make, Model); HIRE(HireID, CustomerID, CarReg, StartDate, Days) (d) less redundancy, fewer update anomalies
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) partial dependency example [1]; non-key dependency example [1] (c) CUSTOMER(CustomerID, CustomerName); CAR(CarReg, Make, Model); HIRE(HireID, CustomerID, CarReg, StartDate, Days) [4] (d) [1]

items.answer: (a) PatientID + DoctorID + AppDate + AppTime (b) partial: PatientName depends only on PatientID; transitive: Specialism depends on DoctorID, which is not the whole key (c) PATIENT(PatientID, PatientName); DOCTOR(DoctorID, DoctorName, Specialism); APPOINTMENT(PatientID, DoctorID, AppDate, AppTime, Room) (d) less redundancy, fewer update anomalies
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) partial dependency example [1]; non-key dependency example [1] (c) PATIENT(PatientID, PatientName); DOCTOR(DoctorID, DoctorName, Specialism); APPOINTMENT(PatientID, DoctorID, AppDate, AppTime, Room) [4] (d) [1]

items.stem: A table in 1NF is also in second normal form (2NF) when
options: it has at least two tables
items.answer: it has no partial dependencies
items.markingKey: 2NF: every non-key attribute depends on the whole primary key.

items.stem: A table in 2NF is in third normal form (3NF) when
options: it has no non-key dependencies (transitive dependencies)
items.answer: it has no non-key dependencies (transitive dependencies)
items.markingKey: 3NF: non-key attributes depend only on the key.

items.stem: Explain how the unnormalised table ORDER(OrderID, OrderDate, CustomerID, CustomerName, CustomerPhone, ProductID, ProductName, UnitPrice, Quantity), used by an online shop, could lead to a insert anomaly.
items.answer: Data about one entity cannot be added until related data exists (e.g. a new item cannot be stored until it appears in a transaction).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: describes the insert problem; 1 mark: linked to the table attributes [2]

items.stem: Explain how the unnormalised table APPOINTMENT(PatientID, PatientName, DoctorID, DoctorName, Specialism, AppDate, AppTime, Room), used by a medical centre, could lead to a update anomaly.
items.answer: If a value such as a name is stored in many records, changing it means updating every copy; missing one leaves inconsistent data.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: describes the update problem; 1 mark: linked to the table attributes [2]

items.stem: What is a data dictionary?
options: A list of all the data values
A file that holds metadata about the database, such as table names, field names, types and validation rules
items.answer: A file that holds metadata about the database, such as table names, field names, types and validation rules
items.markingKey: The data dictionary describes the structure of the data, not the data itself.

items.stem: Explain how a DBMS addresses the problems of a file-based system.
items.answer: Stores data once in related tables (less redundancy and inconsistency); data dictionary describes data independently of programs (data independence); access rights and backup/recovery tools improve security and integrity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point, max 3 [3]

items.stem: Explain why the data dictionary is important for a database developer.
items.answer: It records names, types, sizes, keys and validation rules, so developers can build queries and programs correctly and the DBMS can enforce validation.

items.stem: MetroBus in Kuala Lumpur has grown and now has 30 staff using shared data. Evaluate the benefits to MetroBus of replacing its spreadsheets with a database management system.
items.answer: Points in favour: less redundancy and inconsistency; data independence; access rights; query processor; backup and recovery; multi-user access. items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What is a data dictionary? (b) What is the purpose of the query processor in a DBMS?
items.answer: (a) A file that holds metadata about the database, such as table names, field names, types and validation rules (b) To process and optimise queries so data can be retrieved efficiently
items.markingKey: (a) The data dictionary describes the structure of the data, not the data itself. (b) Query processor interprets and executes queries (e.g. SQL).

items.stem: TransGlobal Logistics in Doha is moving its data into a DBMS. Explain the difference between the logical schema and the data dictionary.
items.answer: The logical schema models the whole database (tables, relationships); the data dictionary stores detailed metadata about each item (names, types, rules).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Nova Telecom in Mumbai uses a DBMS to manage its staff, stock and sales data. Explain the benefit of indexing a frequently searched field.
items.answer: Searches and sorts on that field are faster because the index can be used rather than scanning every record.

items.stem: Eagles Sports Club in Doha has grown and now has 30 staff using shared data. Discuss, with reasons, the benefits to Eagles Sports Club of replacing its spreadsheets with a database management system.
items.answer: Points in favour: less redundancy and inconsistency; data independence; access rights; query processor; backup and recovery; multi-user access. items.stem: What is a candidate key?
options: A foreign key with no matching record
A key that has been deleted
Any field or combination of fields that could be chosen as the primary key
A field that contains only numbers
items.answer: Any field or combination of fields that could be chosen as the primary key
items.markingKey: Candidate keys are unique and minimal; one is chosen as the primary key.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why a primary key is needed in each table. (b) Explain the difference between a primary key and a foreign key.
items.answer: (a) It uniquely identifies each record so records can be found, updated and linked through foreign keys without ambiguity. (b) A primary key uniquely identifies records in its own table; a foreign key is an attribute in another table that refers to that primary key to create a relationship.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: unique identification; 1 mark: linking/searching [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Orbit Games Studio in Madrid keeps customer details in one file for the sales team and a separate file of orders for the warehouse. (a) Describe how a relational database would be structured instead. (b) Explain how referential integrity prevents errors.
items.answer: (a) Separate tables for each entity (CUSTOMER, ORDER) linked by primary/foreign keys; data stored once. (b) Each foreign key must match an existing primary key so an order cannot refer to a customer who does not exist.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark tables; 1 mark keys/link [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: What is a composite key?
options: A key made by joining two tables
A foreign key that is also encrypted
A primary key made of two or more fields
A field that contains text and numbers
items.answer: A primary key made of two or more fields
items.markingKey: e.g. (StudentID, CourseID) in an ENROLMENT table.

items.stem: Explain how the unnormalised table LOAN(MemberID, MemberName, BookID, Title, AuthorID, AuthorName, LoanDate), used by a library, could lead to a update anomaly.
items.answer: If a value such as a name is stored in many records, changing it means updating every copy; missing one leaves inconsistent data.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: describes the update problem; 1 mark: linked to the table attributes [2]

items.stem: Explain how the unnormalised table ENROLMENT(StudentID, StudentName, TutorID, TutorName, CourseID, CourseName, Grade), used by a college, could lead to a insert anomaly.
items.answer: Data about one entity cannot be added until related data exists (e.g. a new item cannot be stored until it appears in a transaction).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: describes the insert problem; 1 mark: linked to the table attributes [2]
